disease_info: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is a trauma- and stressor-related condition that emerges within days of exposure to a severe traumatic event involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation, either directly experienced, witnessed, or learned about occurring to a close other. It is characterized by a cluster of intrusive memories, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, and marked arousal, lasting from at least 3 days up to 1 month after the trauma, and causing significant distress or functional impairment. Clinically, ASD often presents with sudden changes in functioning at work or home, emotional numbing or agitation, and difficulty integrating the traumatic experience into ongoing life. It is distinguished from Posttraumatic Stress Disorder primarily by its shorter duration and more prominent dissociative symptoms early on, though it confers increased risk for later PTSD if symptoms persist or worsen.

narrative.stressor: Two weeks before presentation, Angelina was driving home after a late closing shift at the store when another car ran a red light and T-boned her vehicle at a downtown Honolulu intersection. Although she escaped with only minor physical injuries and the other driver survived, she was trapped in the car for several minutes, surrounded by shattered glass and the smell of burning rubber, while bystanders and first responders worked to get her out. In the days that followed, her usually structured routines around hiking, yoga, and creative work began to unravel, and she found herself increasingly unable to complete merchandising plans or concentrate on digital design tasks she previously enjoyed. After nearly missing an important store reset because she could not bring herself to drive to work and her manager gently confronted her about her sudden drop in performance and focus, her older cousin—who had also noticed her withdrawing from family and cultural activities—encouraged her to see a mental health professional through the clinic affiliated with her employer.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since the car accident I just can’t think straight or focus long enough to finish anything, even simple tasks at work.”

narrative.stressor: About three weeks before seeking care, Anthony was working the night shift at a mid-range hotel off the Las Vegas Strip when an attempted armed robbery occurred in the lobby. He was at the front desk when a masked man pointed a gun directly at him while demanding cash, and he had to lie on the floor with several guests while listening to the assailant threaten to shoot if anyone moved until security intervened and police arrived. In the two weeks afterward, his previously steady performance deteriorated sharply: he began dreading his shifts, struggled to stay present with guests, and his supervisor noted he was making repeated reservation errors and asking to leave early, which was very uncharacteristic for him. After his wife noticed how the incident was affecting his ability to function at home and at the community center where he mentors youth, she insisted he speak with their primary care provider, who referred him for an urgent psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep reliving that night at the front desk over and over in my head, like I’m back on the floor with a gun in my face and I can’t shut it off.”

narrative.stressor: Two weeks before coming to clinic, Dalia was driving back from a pottery circle meeting on a rainy evening when she witnessed a multi-car collision on the freeway near Escondido, including a vehicle that flipped several times and came to rest near her lane. She pulled over and, along with other bystanders, approached the wreckage, seeing severely injured occupants while waiting for emergency services, and briefly assisted a dazed teenager out of a damaged car. In the days that followed, her normally reliable routines—early-morning inventory checks, carefully planned budgets, and weekend hikes—were disrupted as she found herself increasingly on edge and unable to relax even during cooking or pottery, which had always been calming for her. After she started avoiding certain freeway routes to work, arrived late multiple times, and her teenage child commented that she seemed "on another planet" during family dinners, she agreed to schedule an appointment through her health plan after a colleague at the store shared her own experience with trauma counseling.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Since I saw that freeway accident, I feel like I’m moving through life in a fog, like I’m watching myself from the outside and nothing feels quite real.”
